item.title: Cornell rape accuser can remain 'Jane Doe' as judge warns threats could lead to federal charges
item.description: A New York judge ruled the Cornell Jane Doe accuser can keep her pseudonym in the civil case against Chi Phi fraternity members she accused of rape.
item.content:encoded:
A judge has allowed the former Cornell student who sued the Chi Phi fraternity members over rape allegations to continue using the pseudonym "Jane Doe."

New York Supreme Court Justice Phaedra Perry-Bond, who is presiding over the civil case, said in a Friday order that Jane Doe had argued that publicly identifying her could expose her to "retribution and retaliation," hinder her social life and career, and cause shame to her family.

Doe also told the court that she fears being identified would lead to her family being placed in danger, adding that she has "experienced extreme anxiety, depression, and insomnia."

None of the defendants opposed Doe's request to continue using a pseudonym, according to the order.

CORNELL UNIVERSITY BANS FRATERNITY PARTIES FOR THE REST OF THE YEAR AFTER SEX ABUSE LAWSUIT

Ultimately, the judge ruled that Doe's privacy interests outweighed the normal presumption that court proceedings should be fully public, especially given "the notoriety of the allegations" and "the widespread reports of certain malicious actors' behavior in attempting to threaten and retaliate against anyone tangentially involved in this case."

In an unusual move, the judge included a sort of public service announcement in her order, warning that attempts to harass or threaten Doe, the defendants or attorneys involved in the case could constitute a federal crime and lead to prosecution.

Perry-Bond also noted that allowing Doe to use a pseudonym would preserve public access to the case without resorting to more restrictive measures, such as sealing the court docket or closing the courtroom.

While Doe will remain anonymous publicly, the individually named defendants will continue to be identified in court filings.

CORNELL SEXUAL ASSAULT CASE REVIVES SCRUTINY OF A LITTLE-KNOWN NEW YORK LAW ON INTOXICATED VICTIMS

However, Perry-Bond said protections for sensitive personal information, such as home addresses, phone numbers and email addresses, should also be extended to the individually named defendants. She invited the parties to propose an agreement providing similar protections to defendants and potentially other people involved in the case.

Doe filed her lawsuit in September, accusing seven former Chi Phi fraternity members of drugging and raping her on the night of Oct. 19, 2024, and into the next morning.

The complaint also names the fraternity itself, the university, and the bar Doe went to the night of the alleged gang rape.

In the lawsuit, she alleges she was already intoxicated when she arrived at the fraternity house, where the men then pressured her to take ketamine and other substances. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some saying any sexual activity was consensual and others denying they were involved.

BAR NAMED IN CORNELL RAPE LAWSUIT DISPUTES ACCUSER'S ACCOUNT, SAYS SHE WAS NEVER SERVED ALCOHOL WHILE UNDERAGE

The fraternity was suspended on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day Doe reported sexual assault allegations to campus police, according to Doe's civil complaint.

Local prosecutor Matthew Van Houten, who intially declined to pursue criminal charges, has said Doe's sworn statement from November 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang-raped.

That statement, Van Houten said, described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as "voluntary, conscious, and consensual."

However, CBS New York later obtained the transcript of the Cornell police interviews with Doe on Nov. 14 and 15, 2024, during which she told investigators: "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."

SALLY YATES' CORNELL REVIEW OF ALLEGED GANG RAPE COULD SCRUTINIZE CRUCIAL POLICE INTERVIEW, ATTORNEY SAYS

Van Houten said he was never given this full transcript. He announced late last month that his office was reopening the investigation after allegations made in Doe's lawsuit differed from those in her sworn statement nearly two years earlier.

Days after Van Houten reversed course, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul removed him from the case, citing her lack of confidence in his judgment, and appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor.

James' appointment has also drawn controversy, with multiple defendants seeking her removal over alleged bias stemming largely from a social media post she made days before her appointment that they argue showed sympathy for Jane Doe.

On Thursday, James filed a response in court, arguing that the defendants have no standing and that even if they did, the governor has the power to appoint a special prosecutor.

A separate motion from another defendant, a former fraternity member, asked the state Supreme Court to disqualify James from any future grand jury proceedings, arguing that her public comments had prejudiced potential grand jurors and undermined the fairness of the process. That matter remains pending.

item.title: AI hasn’t replaced humans. Employers are still betting on college degrees
item.description: A Gallup poll finds 80% of employers prefer college degree holders, and nearly half say degrees will matter more as artificial intelligence grows.
item.content:encoded:
The current narrative would have you believe that higher education is a dying institution. Experts consistently claim that a four-year degree is no longer worth the investment, warning that artificial intelligence (AI) is on the verge of rendering human labor obsolete. The prevailing message dictates that machines will soon dominate the workforce, leaving the next generation with no viable career paths. But a recent Gallup poll reveals a contrasting reality. While public anxiety is high, the job market tells a different story.

According to a recent Gallup study, a staggering 80% of employers prefer to hire candidates with a college degree, even for roles that do not explicitly require one. Furthermore, 6 in 10 employers express a high level of confidence in higher education. While public trust in institutions has undeniably plummeted, the people actually handing out paychecks still find immense value in the university system.

These hiring managers are acting on current market demands. They recognize an economic reality cultural commentators have missed.

DEMOCRATS SOUND ALARM OVER AI JOB APOCALYPSE — BUT LABOR MARKET ISN'T FOLLOWING SCRIPT

The most fascinating revelation in the data involves our collective panic over artificial intelligence. The dominant cultural narrative repeatedly asserts that generative AI will replace white-collar workers and make higher education irrelevant. Yet, nearly half of the surveyed employers believe that college degrees will actually become more important over the next five years specifically because of AI. Only a quarter believe degrees will lose their value.

The business sector sees this same technological disruption and concludes that formal education is becoming a scarcer but more necessary commodity.

CHRISTIAN UNIVERSITY AIMS TO PRODUCE 'IRREPLACEABLE' GRADUATES AS AI RESHAPES HIGHER EDUCATION

The market is reacting this way because artificial intelligence has exposed the limits of automation. As technical, repetitive tasks become increasingly automated, the value of uniquely human traits is actually skyrocketing. Employers want young professionals who possess relational intelligence, the ability to navigate friction and the resilience to solve complex problems.

When an employer sees a college degree, that business leader sees a certification of competence, but also sees documented proof of hard work. A degree signals that a young adult can commit to a multi-year project, accept critical feedback and collaborate with a diverse team. These are the foundational skills of professionals. They are the skills a machine cannot replicate.

FORTY-FIVE PERCENT OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE CAN BE JUSTIFIED TO STOP HATE SPEECH, POLL FINDS

However, higher education leaders cannot afford to view this survey as the final victory. The fact that employers currently trust universities and colleges does not mean they will always trust them. This data should not be used to justify raising tuition or the construction of resort-style campus amenities. The American university system must continue to evolve and stay relevant in today’s world.

Furthermore, universities must continually guard against intellectual fragility. If institutions prioritize emotional comfort over rigorous debate, they will graduate students who are ill-equipped for a competitive global economy. Employers desire critical thinkers, not activists who demand everyone agree with them. If universities become expensive echo chambers rather than centers of intellectual friction, the results of this survey will be reversed.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

It is telling that the Gallup data shows the lowest confidence in higher education comes from small businesses with fewer than 10 employees. These entrepreneurs are the backbone of the American economy and cannot afford the luxury of a bad hire. They need immediate competence. Universities must bridge this gap by partnering with local businesses and ensuring that academic programs are directly aligned with actual workforce needs.

The fear that technology will erase human relevance in the workplace is unwarranted. Business has clearly stated that it still values the development of the human mind and the resilience built through formal education. Now, the burden of proof is squarely on our institutions. Universities must embrace discipline and continue to shape capable leaders. If we do, we can assure the next generation that their future in the workforce remains secure.

item.title: Woman's life transformed when she rejected fast food and vowed to eat what she grows
item.description: From fast food to garden-to-table living, Carmen Perr shares her best tips for shopping at farmers markets and cooking with seasonal fresh herbs.
item.content:encoded:
Before Carmen Perr was sharing garden-to-table recipes with millions of people, she grew up in a busy household with lots of mouths to feed.

"I grew up eating fast food," Perr, the youngest of six children, told Fox News Digital.

Now a Los Angeles-based creator known as Carmen in the Garden, Perr began honing her green thumb more than a decade ago while working in real estate acquisitions.

AMERICANS ARE MAKING COSTLY GROCERY MISTAKE EVEN BEFORE ENTERING THE STORE, EXPERT WARNS

"I started gardening in my first corporate job as a way to cope with stress and anxiety, and I started with just a few potted herbs," she said. "I didn't know what I was doing, but then it slowly grew over time."

Eventually, as she gained more space, her garden expanded to include fruits and vegetables, prompting her to learn how to cook with ingredients she had never used before.

FROM YELLOWSTONE TO YOSEMITE, NEW COOKBOOK REVEALS RECIPES INSPIRED BY AMERICA'S MOST ICONIC PARKS

"I had never cooked an artichoke until I grew one," she said.

Those lessons paved the way for her forthcoming debut cookbook, "Cook What Grows: Seasonal Recipes & Gardening Wisdom for Everyday Eating."

Perr said the book's roughly 100 recipes aim to "spotlight fresh produce in super flavorful but attainable ways."

GROCERY SHOPPERS MAY BE RELYING ON A 'MISLEADING' CLUE WHEN CHOOSING HEALTHY FOODS

"I think that there's a big misconception that eating seasonally has to be expensive," Perr said. "But when you go to a farmers market or your local grocery store, typically what's in season is the more inexpensive option."

She recommends using your senses to guide your produce picks: Look for vibrant colors, feel whether an item is firm or soft and check that herbs smell fragrant.

"When you pick up a bunch of cilantro, you should immediately be able to smell it," Perr said. 

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

The cooking process starts as soon as you're picking out ingredients, she said, so she encourages shoppers to slow down and take in the experience.

Herbs can do much more than finish a dish, she added. 

Fresh, dried and even seeded forms of the same herb can taste totally different, so Perr encourages home cooks to experiment rather than follow strict rules. She uses fresh oregano steeped in hot oil with feta and makes dill-marinated chicken wings finished with dill salt and a dill dipping sauce. 

"You are getting a full dill immersion in a chicken wing format," she said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Sage's drying quality works well to balance rich, fatty dishes, and it was even traditionally rubbed between the hands as a home remedy for clamminess, Perr said.

For dried herbs, Perr also recommends crushing them in your hand before adding them to a dish to help release their oils. 

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Crushing it before you add it to something will explode the flavor," she said.

Her overarching goal is to help people feel more connected to the food they cook. 

"I'm hoping to inspire people to cook what grows, but in turn, grow what they cook," she said.

item.title: Alabama man allegedly decapitates family members with chainsaw hours after 911 warning
item.description: Thomas Henry Steele faces capital murder charges after allegedly killing two family members with a chainsaw at a Mobile, Alabama, home.
item.content:encoded:
An Alabama man is accused of decapitating two family members with a chainsaw after a relative called 911 about his behavior.

Prosecutors are now weighing whether courtroom remarks warrant additional criminal charges after the Mobile man allegedly told a judge to kill his court-appointed attorney.

Thomas Henry Steele, 47, is facing two counts of capital murder in the Oct. 12 deaths of his aunt, Christy Deloach, 65, and grandmother, Dora Boone, 85, at their home on Carolina Court in Mobile.

During an Oct. 13 bond hearing and initial court hearing, Circuit Judge S. Wesley Pipes ordered an inpatient competency evaluation after Steele said "kill him" when the judge appointed public defender Glenn Davidson to represent him.

SUSPECTED FLORIDA PUBLIX SLASHER WALKED FREE FROM COURT MONTHS EARLIER DESPITE VICTIM WARNINGS

Davidson confirmed with Fox News Digital that he is still representing Steele, but does not have additional details to share while Steele undergoes a mental competency evaluation.

"It’s a terrible situation but I won’t have an official way to question anybody until we get to the preliminary hearing," Davidson said.

Tara Zieman, communications director for the Mobile County District Attorney’s Office, told Fox News Digital that prosecutors "have not decided" whether to pursue additional charges over the threat, pending the mental health results.

"The defendant is currently being held without bond at a secure medical facility, where he is receiving treatment intended to restore his competency to stand trial," Zieman said.

"If he is found competent, we will move forward with the prosecution and continue to advocate that he remain held without bond until resolution of the case."

The evaluation, according to the DA’s office, could take up to 90 days and will be carried out at the Alabama Department of Mental Health.

KENTUCKY MAN ENTERS INSANITY PLEA AFTER ADMITTING TO BEATING HIS GRANDMOTHER TO DEATH IN RECORDED ATTACK

"Patients begin receiving restoration and treatment services immediately upon admission," Malissa Valdes, the Public Information Officer for ADMH, told Fox News Digital in an emailed statement.

"Patients are referred for their evaluation once their symptoms are stable and they have completed the restoration program. This timeframe varies based on the patient’s treatment, clinical needs, and their symptoms."

NORTH DAKOTA MOM STABS HER 2 CHILDREN TO DEATH IN 'HORRIFIC' KILLING THAT LEFT COPS TRAUMATIZED: OFFICIALS

Hours before police discovered the women’s bodies, a relative called 911 concerning Steele’s behavior.

According to a 911 transcript obtained by AL.com, the caller said Steele had stopped taking lithium, given away his phone and discussed giving away his vehicle. She described him as bipolar and said he planned to "live for God."

"He’s calm. He’s not violent or anything," she told the dispatcher.

The caller also mentioned contacting 988. The dispatcher provided her with the non-emergency Mobile police number before the call ended.

A criminal complaint alleges that Steele killed both women with a chainsaw, NBC 15 News reported. Police discovered the victims deceased inside the residence and detained Steele at the scene.

Zieman told Fox News Digital that she was unsure whether the victims or other family members made any previous legal attempts to commit Steele for mental health observation.

Steele’s prior incarcerations included "several DUI cases, the most recent dating to 2009," according to Zieman.

Steele is scheduled for arraignment Nov. 19 at 9 a.m. before Mobile County Circuit Court Judge Jay York.

Deloach spent 15 years working at Mr. Sam’s Hair Fashions in Mobile, where salon owner Lenny Zanghi described her as a hardworking stylist who lifted others’ spirits.

"Just a real sweet girl. Beautiful person. I considered her a friend. You know, she’d been with us for 15 years, and she cut my hair," Zanghi told WKRG.

She also cared for her mother, Dora, after her father, Phillip Boone, died. The Boone couple purchased the home in 2014, Lagniappe Daily reported.

item.title: Former Disney star Christy Carlson Romano thought she was 'going to die' after freak shooting accident
item.description: Christy Carlson Romano reveals birdshot remains lodged a millimeter from critical structures near her eye after a clay pigeon shooting accident in Texas.
item.content:encoded:
Christy Carlson Romano is hoping to preserve her vision after a clay pigeon shooting accident in 2025 left birdshot lodged near her eye, putting her at risk of blindness.

"I was peppered with birdshot at about 250 feet away, and I was struck in a fat pocket under my eye, and also in my forehead," Romano told Fox News Digital. "I still have birdshot behind my eye about a millimeter away from anything critical. And if it were to move, I would go blind. So we're hoping that doesn't happen."

The former Disney child star opens up about navigating childhood fame and toxic relationships in her memoir, "Once Upon a Trainwreck." She also recounts being struck by birdshot during the outing in Texas.

DISNEY ALUM CHRISTY CARLSON ROMANO RIPS HOLLYWOOD FOR FAILING CHILD STARS AFTER HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S DEATH

" ... I, at one point, thought that I was going to die," the "Even Stevens" and "Kim Possible" star shared. " ... And when you have children, you can't help but start to see the world completely differently after an accident like that."

Romano's husband, Brendan Rooney, was celebrating his birthday when the couple decided to go clay pigeon shooting.

"In Texas, it's quite common for people to be able to do these sorts of things," Romano said. "And I said, 'Well, you're a former Marine. You're going to enjoy this. Let's go do this.' And unfortunately, there was another part of our party that didn't choose to be responsible with their firearm and fired too closely in my direction."

WATCH: DISNEY STAR CHRISTY CARLSON ROMANO RECALLS TERRIFYING SHOOTING

Clay pigeon shooting is an outdoor sport in which circular clay targets are launched into the air for shooters to hit with shotguns that fire small pellets.

In her memoir, Romano wrote that she collapsed in front of the group and thought, "Am I dead? ... Oh God — my girls."

Romano wrote that her vision blurred as a "dark liquid" appeared to spread across her contact lenses.

As Rooney and the unidentified shooter, whom Romano described as remorseful, rushed to her aid, she wrote that she looked "up at my husband of over 10 years. It's been a good run, right?"

"The Texas sky is big and beautiful today," she wrote. "Cicadas haven't quite woken up from their long winter's nap this February, and it's not too hot or humid. It's a beautiful day to die."

Romano wrote that she became increasingly lightheaded as Rooney urged her not to fall asleep.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Romano recalled the drive to the hospital in her memoir, writing, " ... I try to break the tension as we fly down an empty freeway, going well over the speed limit — 112 miles per hour, to be exact."

"My oculoplastic surgeon had said that, usually, he's taking people's eyes out, kids, because they've been shot with a Nerf gun," Romano told Fox News Digital. "It just so happened to hit the right fat pocket right under the eye. And I really almost survived through a miracle because I think there was any amount of outcomes when it came to having birdshot striking my skull and my face."

Romano wrote, "I'd have a scar and two pieces of birdshot permanently in my head, but I'd live. That's all that mattered." She said doctors determined that removing the fragments would be too risky, so they were left in place.

Romano's oculoplastic surgeon, Dr. Sean Paul, previously explained that the birdshot entered beneath her eye and became lodged in bone farther back, narrowly missing her eyeball, optic nerve and eye muscles by about a millimeter. Paul said she also suffered a subconjunctival hemorrhage, or bleeding beneath the membrane covering the white of the eye, but the pellet did not penetrate the eyeball.

Romano described her recovery as "pretty miraculous." She also thanked the medical staff at St. David's South Austin Medical Center in Austin, Texas, for their care.

"The biggest lesson that I took away from that experience was that life is short, and you need to be really attuned to what it is that you want out of life," Romano explained. "And you need to have a good life. I'd lived such a chaotic lifestyle up until I became a mom that I think it really had me start to reflect even more with the book and exactly how I lived my life up until then. I think that's what gave me the impetus to write my letters to my daughters in the book."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Romano said she was compelled to write her memoir because "after turning 40, I experienced a lot of health scares." In February 2026, the "Vulnerable" podcast host revealed on Instagram that she had received a positive result from a cancer screening.

Romano and Rooney underwent cancer screenings because of her family's history of the disease. Both of her parents had cancer. Her mother survived, but her father died of the disease. Her maternal grandmother also died of lung cancer. Rooney's screening result was negative.

Surviving the shooting and facing the possibility of losing her vision have given Romano a renewed sense of purpose, she said.

"My life today is one that's really focused on personal growth," she said. "I think that my faith has become very big to me, and I have been praying just to really understand my calling and my purpose. And I really believe that if the book could help people feel a little less alone, that it would have been worth all of my vulnerability and all of my sharing. And I'm hoping the right people find it."

Fox News Digital's Ashley Hume contributed to this report.

item.title: Steve Sarkisian could face college football's hardest call as Arch Manning invokes much higher stakes
item.description: Steve Sarkisian's Texas Longhorns have spent over $40 million to contend for a title, but Saturday's Ole Miss game now feels like a season-defining test.
item.content:encoded:
I don’t imagine Steve Sarkisian thought, three months ago at SEC Media Days, that Texas’ 2026 season would hinge on one October game amid growing concerns about Arch Manning’s struggles on offense.

At the time, Sarkisian was discussing the Longhorns’ need to break through the College Football Playoff semifinals. Now, the conversation surrounding Texas centers on whether Arch Manning can make it through Saturday night’s showdown against Ole Miss without Sarkisian being forced to turn to backup KJ Lacey.

"He's very comfortable with who he is. He's not trying to be something that he's not," Sarkisian said at SEC Media Days about Manning.

DID WE CREATE A MONSTER? ARCH MANNING 'AW SHUCKS' PERSONA IS SUPPOSEDLY GONE BEFORE CRITICAL OLE MISS SHOWDOWN

Unfortunately for those that have rooting interest on 'Forty Acres' in the football program, we have reached the point where this has become a must-win game against Ole Miss, for a Longhorns team that continues to struggle on offense without many answers on how to fix it, besides letting Arch "rip it."

Looking back to those conversations in Tampa before the season started, Arch Manning is now trying to be something he's not by taking on an "edgy" mindset with his perceived back against the wall.

Or maybe it's the opposite. Has Manning always been a young man that carried an edge about him, until Sarkisian tamed him?

Either way, Steve Sarkisian has noticed something different about his quarterback this week, which also comes at a time of heightened criticism towards the Texas offense.

"I don’t know if we lost him. We created this. We did. All of us. Y’all included. Me. The whole thing, right. Everybody on ESPN, we’ve created this. And so we’ll see what comes out of it," Sarkisian said about Manning's persona this week.

STEVE SARKISIAN VOWS TO 'EVALUATE EVERYTHING,' WON’T RULE OUT BENCHING ARCH MANNING AMID TEXAS' TWO-GAME SKID

A loss to the Rebels inside DKR Stadium on Saturday would all but seal the fate of this Texas team that has spent over $40 million in hopes of contending for a national championship this season.

Instead, the situation in Austin has taken a dramatic turn over the past three weeks.

Consecutive losses to unranked opponents — including a debacle against Florida — have forced staffers inside the football facility to operate with a sense of urgency. Meanwhile, those outside the program are wondering whether Manning and Sarkisian can finally produce a performance that matches the hype.

Yes, the fourth-quarter comeback win against Ohio State still carries weight in terms of upcoming CFP rankings.

But, with the subdued offensive numbers that Sarkisian and Arch Manning have produced over the past month, the pressure has now reached a fever pitch within the Texas fan base.

What does the Longhorns quarterback do with the pressure mounting on this offense to finally break through the fourth wall with enough firepower to keep up with an team like Ole Miss?

"Just letting it rip," Arch Manning said this week. "Our backs are against the wall right now, and there's no place I'd rather be. Just let her rip. I'm going to die on the hill of, I'm letting it rip."

No more thinking, just doing. That's the plan for a Texas offense that should be three steps ahead of its current state, if you factor in the amount of talent that takes the field on every drive.

STEVE SARKISIAN’S ‘JOE SMITH’ ARGUMENT FOR ARCH MANNING IS ABSOLUTE NONSENSE FOR AN AVERAGE QB

The problem for this offense doesn’t just solely fall at the hands of Arch Manning, as Sarkisian has to rightfully take plenty of the blame. This scheme feels bland, compared to what it might actually look like within the playbook.

"I think there’s no doubt about it, Arch can play better for us," Sarkisian said on Monday. "He’s our starter, but I need to see a better version of Arch Manning like I need to see a better version of a lot of guys on our offensive football team right now, but we need to see a better version of him this week."

But, what if Manning is just an average quarterback with a last name that is a cornerstone of football?

There's nothing wrong with that, and the conversation around Arch is warranted based off the perceived talent that is within in. At the end of the day, though, the only thing we can rely on is what we see on a weekly basis out of Texas...

Appearing on the Craig Carton show this week, former NFL quarterback Ryan Leaf had a blunt answer regarding what he has seen from Arch Manning this season and whether he should return for another year of college ball.

"I think Texas is a great spot for him because the talent is so rich and they're going to have a great football team," Leaf mentioned. But listen, he's an average college quarterback. Even more so because of how talented his teammates are. It doesn’t mean he's bad.

"Does he have the DNA to become better and continue to get better? Of course he does. It would such a mistake for someone to draft him high. If another year allows him to get better and improve, then do it..."

Now comes the biggest test of the Sarkisian-Manning era at Texas.

A showdown with Ole Miss that will determine whether we are still talking about the Longhorns as a legit contender for the college football playoff once the first rankings are announced in just a few weeks.

And they will have to do it against a Pete Golding defense that is looking to stay on its own path towards the postseason behind an offense that actually seems to have its stuff together behind Trinidad Chambliss.

There is no way we will see another weekend of chaos like what we witnessed last Saturday, right?

If you haven’t figured it out by now, parity has finally wreaked havoc on a sport that is filled with $35 to $45 million rosters.

And sometimes, it just comes down to a situation not working out. For instance, I don't imagine folks in Ann Arbor would be wondering why Michigan would be forced to bench a quarterback it signed out of high school with a contract worth millions.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

But, Bryce Underwood wasn’t cutting it, so now the Wolverines turn to freshman Tommy Carr for a showdown against No. 6 Indiana that could ultimately be a trap for a Hoosiers team coming off a close loss to Ohio State.

Is there an upset brewing in Michigan? Based off what we have seen this season around college football, nothing is off the table.

There might even come a time on Saturday when the Wolverines have to give Underwood the ball back, if the Carr experiment doesn’t come to fruition as the coaching staff is hoping.

Either way, the expensive marriage between Michigan and Bryce Underwood feels as though it coming to an end in Ann Arbor, with a contract clause that will allow the Wolverines to go their separate way following the 2026 season without financial penalty.

Unfortunately, though, this is the gamble you take on a high school quarterback that shows a lot of potential, but there is zero evidence to show that they will be successful at the collegiate level.

In a way, it's as if worlds are colliding between the Texas and Michigan football programs in terms of quarterbacks.

A lot of promise. A lot of money spent on making sure they compete for a title. But two programs living on different spectrums of chaos this season.

In other words, college football in 2026.

item.title: I could have rescued my daughter from disappointment. Here's why I didn't
item.description: A child psychologist explains why rescuing kids from disappointment undermines self-efficacy, coping skills, and long-term child resilience.
item.content:encoded:
A few weeks ago, my daughter came home from second grade, and she told me she wasn’t invited to her friend Samantha’s birthday party. I asked her if she knew how many kids were invited, and she told me twenty. I was incensed. It was a big party, not a small, exclusive gathering, and my baby was left out. I knew that, in that moment, I could do two things: acknowledge that being left out hurts, or pick up the phone and call Samantha’s mom to secure an invitation. I had to deliberately focus on the former and stop myself from instinctually choosing the latter because, these days, it seems like we are all defaulting to the phone call.

The instinct is understandable. We all hate watching our children suffer. But we need to remember that there is a clear difference between supporting our children through disappointment and making sure they never experience it.

OUR KIDS AREN’T BROKEN. WE NEED TO STOP TREATING EVERY STRUGGLE LIKE A DISORDER

It seems like we have lost our ability to tolerate ordinary childhood struggles. We pathologize and diagnose every negative experience—sadness becomes depression, meanness becomes bullying, and frustration becomes emotional dysregulation. And each unsavory, undesirable part of life becomes an intervention target. Parents feel pressure to act rather than simply let life unfold.

But the reality is that life is messy and often uncomfortable, and not every negative emotion is evidence of a problem that requires us to intervene. Emotional discomfort isn’t inherently dangerous, and, in fact, negative experiences can serve important developmental functions. Coping with adversity helps kids recognize what matters to them, adjust expectations, solve problems, and navigate relationships. When we have a myopic focus on protecting children’s mental health, we often forget that mental health is based not on the absence of negative emotions but on our ability to handle them.

As parents, we must remember that resilience requires practice, and competence develops through experience. Children build coping skills when they encounter manageable challenges, experiment with solutions, and discover that they can tolerate discomfort. And all this requires the possibility of failure. Children never develop the ability to recover from disappointment if they don’t have the opportunity to feel it.

I WORRY LESS ABOUT SCREENS THAN ABOUT THE CHALLENGES TODAY’S TEENS NEVER FACE

Parents have a key role to play in the development of self-efficacy. We communicate our expectations about what they can do. When we give our children space to learn and grow, we communicate that they can handle challenges on their own. On the flip side, when we repeatedly intervene to solve their problems, we send the message that they can’t do it without us. It’s impossible to teach kids to swim by keeping them out of the water!

Constantly rescuing our kids has three unintended consequences. First, it undermines self-efficacy. Children look to adults to solve problems rather than trusting themselves and discovering their own resourcefulness. Second, it reinforces avoidance. Children learn that unpleasant emotions are intolerable rather than temporary experiences that they can manage. Third, it creates unrealistic expectations. Children learn to expect the world to accommodate their preferences rather than learning to manage unfairness, frustration, rejection, and disappointment.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Of course, children often need support. Removing demands may, at times, be necessary. But when we reflexively remove demands instead of helping children develop the capacity to navigate them, we prioritize short-term relief over long-term growth.

We must deliberately support our children without constantly rescuing them. First, we should validate the feeling without catastrophizing it. Acknowledge the disappointment, but don’t amplify it into a crisis. Second, resist the urge to solve the problem. Before intervening, ask whether it is something your child can reasonably navigate independently. Third, help your child develop their own solutions. You can ask them what they could do next or what they might try differently next time, but remember that sometimes the best intervention is no intervention at all. Sometimes children just need time to feel bad and move on.

When I think about my own daughter and that birthday party, I wonder if maybe this will give her the opportunity and motivation to make a new friend. Maybe she’ll learn to cope with exclusion. Maybe she’ll just feel bummed for the afternoon and move on. All are developmentally meaningful (and desirable) outcomes. And I remember that my job isn’t to eliminate adversity and disappointment; it’s to help her become a person who can handle the struggles that are inevitably part of life.

I don’t want to raise someone who never falls down; I want to raise someone who knows how to get back up.

item.title: Canada is feeling the pain from Trump's tariffs — but the trade fight didn't start overnight
item.description: President Donald Trump's trade showdown with Canada targets dairy, lumber and market access, reviving decades-old tensions between allied economies.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump's escalating trade fight with Canada is squeezing the economy north of the border, threatening jobs and adding to families' financial strain as steep U.S. tariffs on roughly $20 billion in goods remain in place.

U.S. tariffs have hammered the country's steel, aluminum, lumber and automobile producers that depend heavily on the American market. Steel exports have fallen by roughly half since the tariffs took effect, while lumber exports were about 20% below 2024 levels earlier this year, according to the Bank of Canada. Production and jobs have also declined in some of the hardest-hit industries.

Canadian families are feeling the squeeze, too. Consumer prices were 3% higher in August than a year earlier, with grocery prices up 2.8% and transportation costs jumping 7.5%, according to the government's own data.

A MUST-WIN MIDTERM STATE IS THE REAL LOSER OF TRUMP'S CANADA TRADE WAR

Retaliatory tariffs on American products have also added to those costs.

Prices of affected goods, which includes groceries, household products, furniture, electronics and appliances, rose roughly 6% more than comparable products that were not hit by the tariffs, according to the country's central bank.

But while Canada is feeling the economic pain, the disputes driving Trump's trade fight are not new.

"The Trump administration is complaining about dairy access and, generally speaking, those complaints are completely valid," David Clement, North American affairs manager at the Consumer Choice Center, told Fox News Digital.

"Canada has exorbitant tariffs on imports from the United States and really from everywhere around the world when it comes to chicken, turkey, eggs, cheese and milk," Clement said.

THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE

Clement noted, however, that differences between American and European access to Canada's market reflect terms negotiated under separate trade agreements, including the USMCA struck during Trump's first term.

But dairy represents just a fraction of the broader U.S.-Canada trading relationship.

Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics at the Cato Institute and the Herbert A. Stiefel Center for Trade Policy Studies, said more than 99% of U.S.-Canada trade was duty-free before 2025, with negotiators historically willing to tolerate disputes over politically sensitive products like dairy to preserve the broader relationship.

"The Trump administration has so far refused to make the deal," he said.

Lincicome said free trade in products including fertilizer, energy and lumber helps keep costs down for American farmers, homebuilders and consumers.

With the midterm elections just weeks away and the cost of living in focus, the trade dispute is unfolding as higher energy prices add another layer of pressure on consumers.

Lincicome called the combination a "double whammy."

"First you had the tariffs which increased the prices of a lot of products. And then you had energy prices spike because of the Iran war," he said.

Higher diesel prices can ripple through the economy because they fuel tractors, trucks and trains, Lincicome said, acting "as kind of another tariff" by raising the cost of getting products to consumers.

Despite the escalating tensions, Clement cautioned against allowing the dispute to undermine the broader relationship.

"The partnership between Canada and the United States is one of the greatest trading relationships the world has ever known," he said. "That should be embraced. It should be enhanced, and it shouldn't be torn down by either side."

item.title: DEPROGRAMMED: He was headed for the MLB. Instead he stepped up to the plate for God
item.description: Nehemiah Toles walked away from top college baseball offers and MLB scouts after hearing God's voice in a hotel room following a championship game.
item.content:encoded:
Star outfielder Nehemiah Toles had multiple Division-I college baseball offers and MLB scouts watching him as he neared high school graduation, but he turned all of it down in pursuit of his purpose — preaching the Gospel to bring America’s youth to Jesus.

"It's the scariest thing to be gifted at something that God did not call you to… Baseball was my passion, it wasn't my purpose," Toles told Fox News Digital.

"When I stand before God… and he looks at me, he's gonna say well done, good and faithful servant. How did hitting home runs, how would that have served Him?" he continued.

FALCONS ROOKIE ZACHARIAH BRANCH SAYS CHRISTIAN FAITH, DAILY DEVOTIONALS FUEL HIS NFL JOURNEY

Toles, who now runs his own ministry traveling across the U.S. to preach the Gospel, grew up in a household with a pastor father transitioning to be an evangelist. Although surrounded by faith in his home, he admits to thinking religion and following God was "corny" during his youth.

The former baseball player revealed that he used the sport as a "coping mechanism" while dealing with anxiety and depression that peaked in school during the pandemic of 2020.

"From 13 years old to 16 years old… I felt like I struggled to connect with people, struggled to just articulate my thoughts. And so… I went back to church, [and] before I even started worshiping or anything like that, I felt the presence of God just hit me. All my anxiety, all my depression left, and I had tried everything else and nothing else was working," Toles continued.

JUST 5 MINUTES OF PRAYER COULD HAVE SURPRISING HEALTH BENEFITS, STUDY FINDS

Toles detailed one of his first experiences receiving college offers during a championship game while ranked the top outfielder in the state of Ohio, running to second base chalking up reddish brown dust in the air with the impact of each cleated step, seeing his coach on the phone from under the shadow of his baseball cap, rounding third base and finishing a home run before making it to the dugout.

"I'm in the dugout. And [my coach] he's like… before [you] touched home plate, three Division-I coaches had just confirmed," Toles continued.

He described the elation on his parents' faces and recalled his father’s tears at the news of the offers from Yale and a handful of other universities, all right before he heard the voice of God later that night alone in his room.

LOUISIANA FOOTBALL PHENOM PEYTON HOUSTON CREDITS FAITH, FAMILY FOR HIS REMARKABLE SUCCESS

"[In] the hotel room that night and I felt like the Lord had spoke[n] to me, like, 'Is that enough? Was that what you were looking for? Like, is this ever, is it going to be enough?'" he said.

Toles described serving at a community event helping children in need shortly after that game, wrestling between both destinies, finding that serving those kids was "something deeper" and "more satisfying" to him than hitting home runs or getting top college offers.

"I felt like God was calling me into full-time ministry and so… [During that] exact event, I went back to the green room and I called half of the Division-I coaches and told them I'm not going to come to their college, I'm going full-time into ministry," Toles said.

NFL LINEBACKER AND AMATEUR PREACHER DEMARIO DAVIS DELIVERS AMAZING SERMON ON WINNING AND LIFE

Despite tension with his family and multiple hard conversations with various adults, from guidance counselors to coaches and more imploring Toles to reconsider his decision, he stood firm.

TONY DUNGY TELLS SAGE STEELE THAT NBC WASN'T HAPPY WITH HIS PRO-LIFE VIEWS: 'THEY KNEW WHERE I STOOD'

"Everything that the world had offered me didn't satisfy me… I remember feeling so deceived and feeling so frustrated, because doing the things that people had told me to do [that] they said they would make me happy and would fulfill me… didn't," he added.

Toles endured pressure from all sides that eventually led him to question his choice, but when he asked God, he heard his voice clearer than ever.

"He made it so evident to me, He [said], obedience to me will always be insanity to the world," Toles said.

item.title: Jon Bon Jovi impersonator uses AI videos to scam woman out of $10K, nearly costing her home
item.description: Leslie Pickett lost over $10,000 to a deepfake scam after a fake Jon Bon Jovi account on Instagram used AI videos to build trust over months.
item.content:encoded:
She gave love a chance. A scammer gave it a bad name.

For months, Leslie Pickett thought she was talking to Jon Bon Jovi, the rock star she had adored since she was 14. The man behind the screen messaged her day and night, sent convincing videos and eventually persuaded her to hand over thousands of dollars.

By the time the deception unraveled, she had lost more than $10,000 and came close to losing her home.

WOMAN LOSES NEARLY $1M IN LINKEDIN ROMANCE SCAM

"My heart was shattered," the Louisiana resident told Fox News Digital. "I was still willing to give him the benefit of the doubt. But there was nothing but ill intent. That's what hurt the most."

Pickett's story is featured in the National Geographic documentary special "Super Scam Me," in which Emmy Award-winning journalist Mariana van Zeller goes undercover to investigate online scams, traveling to Africa to confront a suspected scammer face-to-face.

"We're living in the era of scams," van Zeller told Fox News Digital. "Romance scams, in particular, are the fastest growing, and I believe, most devastating form of financial crime out there. One in seven Americans have reported losing money to romance scams. And so, I think now is the best time to raise awareness."

WATCH: Woman warns of SIM swap scam after hackers drained her bank account

Fox News Digital reached out to Bon Jovi’s spokesperson for comment.

Pickett, who was "more of a Facebook person," was introduced to Instagram by her daughter. She came across Bon Jovi's verified account in late 2024 and commented on one of his posts. Five minutes later, she received a response from an account that appeared to belong to Bon Jovi himself. However, the account wasn't verified.

"He gave very thoughtful answers to my questions, so I genuinely thought it was him," Pickett said. "And I wasn't too knowledgeable about those check marks. I had doubts, but hey, a girl can dream."

According to Pickett, the impostor told her Bon Jovi wanted to connect with his fans more personally. He also warned that if Bon Jovi's management discovered the secret account, it would be shut down.

For months, the two exchanged messages "several times a day and several times at night," bonding over music and common interests. According to Pickett, the impostor remembered details from their earliest conversations, told her "I love you" and even sent a bouquet of flowers to her home. He also sent recorded videos, and the two eventually connected on a live video call.

Pickett, who had no idea he was generative AI to play the rock star, was convinced she was talking to Bon Jovi. The scammer also claimed that he and his wife had quietly filed for divorce but were keeping it under wraps to protect his public image.

Pickett showed the photos and videos to her cousin, who was skeptical that Bon Jovi would be in a secret relationship with a fan. But after seeing the images, he reportedly exclaimed, "That's him! There's no doubt about it."

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"It was like talking to my best friend," Pickett said. "He said he wanted to meet someone normal. He didn't want somebody that wanted fame, money and things like that. So, we didn't really talk about stuff like that. We talked about everyday life. I had my doubts, but I was praying it was him."

Months later, the man posing as Bon Jovi started asking for money.

"He had an exclusive performance in Nashville, where he only let a thousand people buy tickets," Pickett recalled. "The show was legitimate. Unfortunately, I tried to buy tickets, but they sold out in four minutes. When I told him about it, he suggested a meet and greet. He had never asked me for money before. He said, 'To get you in the meet and greet, you're going to have go through management since there are no tickets left.’ He gave me emails to his management, and he walked me through how to do everything. I've never even heard of the word 'crypto.’"

"That was a red flag, but the money was given with intent," Pickett continued. "I was supposed to get something in return. Meet and greets are also a common thing with famous people so I didn't see it as scammy at all. The bitcoin and crypto were the only things that made me go, 'Why am I not logging into a regular site?' He said, 'Those get hacked all the time. This is the safest way to do it.' He put me at ease."

The requests for money started small but added up over time. Pickett sent $100 or $150 at a time, only to be told the payments hadn't gone through. The impostor then instructed her to send larger amounts through different payment methods, including Venmo, PayPal, Cash App and cryptocurrency. When one method supposedly failed, she would try another, sometimes staying up at night trying to figure out how to send the money.

"Nothing felt abnormal until I realized the money wasn't coming back into my account," Pickett said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE TRUE CRIME NEWSLETTER

Van Zeller described the scammer’s interactions with Pickett as a "slow burn."

"At first approach, it started as a normal conversation," van Zeller explained. "People think he approached her and said, ‘Hi, I’m Jon Bon Jovi. I’m madly in love with you. Send me money.’ That’s not the case. It took him seven months before he asked Leslie for money. Many people think, ‘How can you give money to a stranger?’ But for Leslie, and many other victims, this was at a point when he wasn’t a stranger. With some victims, they speak to scammers for months, even years."

Advances in artificial intelligence made the deception even harder to detect.

"I had the chance of watching some of the videos that the fake Jon Bon Jovi sent Leslie," van Zeller said. "At one point during this experiment, I was dating three George Clooneys, several Brad Pitts and a few Keanu Reeves. A few sent me videos that were very bad, but some were very good. I received one video from a fake George Clooney that you can watch in the documentary that looked very real. These weren't the old deep fake videos of the past that are full of distortions. These looked professional, believable."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

"In the videos, he would say my name," Pickett recalled. "He would send me videos all the time. One time, I told him, 'Pull on your right ear, cross your eyes and stick your tongue out.' He would send me that within five minutes. That's how good AI is."

In July 2025, the scammer told Pickett he was flying to Louisiana for a meet and greet. He sent her photos of himself seated at a table in a hotel she recognized. The light fixtures, furniture, carpet, utensils and even the napkin rings all matched.

SEND US A TIP

According to Pickett, the scammer told her they needed to complete a security clearance check through Google Chat before they could finally meet in person. When Pickett tried to join the video call, he abruptly hung up. He texted her afterward, claiming there was a security breach because his management believed she was trying to record the call.

The impostor then told Pickett that if she was willing to pay more money to his management, they could arrange another security check, and he would even remain in town for a while. This time, he requested a much larger amount of Bitcoin.

"At that point, I thought, 'Oh my God, this is just not real,'" Pickett said. "That's when my heart sank because I knew I had been duped. That's when I decided to reach out to Mariana for help."

Even after realizing she had been deceived, Pickett wondered whether the man she had been talking to for months was someone living in the United States who genuinely cared about her — someone who wasn't interested only in money but wanted a meaningful relationship.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Van Zeller and Pickett teamed up with a former hacker who helped them trace the scammer's internet protocol (IP) address. The hacker set a trap designed to lure the impostor into claiming more Bitcoin. The IP address led them to Lagos, Nigeria. They then used Google Earth to identify what they believed was the house from which the scammer had been messaging Pickett.

By then, Pickett said she had lost "over $10,000" to the scam. She had fallen so deeply into debt that her home was facing foreclosure.

"I was devastated," Pickett said. "By then I was starting to suspect he was fake. But when Mariana got confirmation, it rocked my world. He could have just come clean, but he just took advantage of my kindness. That's what crushed me."

Today, Pickett is still rebuilding her finances while working a full-time job. She said the emotional toll has been even harder to overcome, leaving her struggling to trust others. She has also become an advocate for scam victims, using social media to warn others about the dangers of interacting with unverified accounts.

"My ultimate goal today is to slow it down and eventually stop this industry," Pickett said. "It devastated my family. It devastated me. It put me in financial dire straits. It affected me emotionally. I wanted to crawl under a rock. No one should ever feel that way. I would never want anyone to go through what I went through."

item.title: Trump officials warn decades-long decline among American men could carry national security consequences
item.description: President Donald Trump's administration develops testosterone screening for troops as an HHS official warns 77% of young Americans can't serve.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration is targeting testosterone deficiency as a potential threat to military readiness, rolling out new screening guidelines for male service members amid growing concerns about the health of American men and the shrinking pool of young people qualified to serve.

"There is absolutely a national defense readiness ramifications for [low testosterone]," Adm. Brian Christine, a senior Department of Health and Human Services official, told Fox News Digital in an interview.

Christine also pointed to broader health challenges facing the military's recruiting pool, warning that 77% of Americans ages 17 to 24 do not qualify for service without a waiver, with obesity, chronic disease and other barriers contributing to the problem. Among young men, he said, more than 70% are ineligible, while only about 3% of young Americans express interest in serving.

The warning comes as the Trump administration places a renewed emphasis on military readiness, with Christine helping shape an initiative that led the Pentagon to issue testosterone deficiency screening guidelines for male service members ages 30 and older in September.

THE REAL REASON BEHIND HEGSETH'S VIRAL MILITARY TESTOSTERONE SCREENING ORDER

Trump entered his second term with an aggressive approach to rebuilding the American military, tightening fitness requirements, axing DEI policies, overhauling weapons acquisition, building up recruitment and refocusing the force on combat readiness and lethality.

Christine, a urologist who spent more than 35 years specializing in men's health, said testosterone levels have been declining for decades, raising concerns about the long-term health of American men and the physical demands placed on those serving in uniform.

"I think it's incredibly important, incredibly timely," Christine said of the screening guidance.

Under the Pentagon's guidelines, male service members ages 30 and older undergo mandatory screening for testosterone deficiency, beginning with an assessment of symptoms and risk factors, with further testing and potential treatment available when medically appropriate.

'WOKE' MILITARY ACADEMIES TARGETED IN NEW BLUEPRINT FOR SWEEPING WARFIGHTING OVERHAUL

"We're not forcing testosterone on anybody," Christine said. "But what we are doing is screening, taking those men who are symptomatic and have low numbers and offering them a pathway forward."

The HHS official pointed to obesity and chronic disease as established factors associated with low testosterone, while raising concerns that environmental exposures, including microplastics and other toxins, could also be contributing to the decline — a possibility researchers are still investigating.

"In the mid-1970s, the average testosterone level for men in this country... was well over 650. Now it's approaching 350," Christine said.

POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO UNEXPECTED MALE FERTILITY BENEFIT

National Institutes of Health Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya echoed those concerns in a separate interview with Fox News Digital, warning that some testosterone deficiency may be going undiagnosed even as medical guidelines stress that a diagnosis requires both symptoms and consistently low hormone levels.

"It's interesting because if you look at the epidemiological trends, testosterone levels in the American male population have been declining over the last decades. And again, we don't know why. We don't have an answer," Bhattacharya said.

Bhattacharya said researchers must determine not only why testosterone levels are declining, but also what medical guidance should follow for men diagnosed with a deficiency. "There are under-diagnosed testosterone deficiencies."

"The question of what to do about it, how to prevent it, that's at the top of my mind," he added.

LONGER LIVES, WORSE HEALTH? SCIENTISTS UNCOVER TROUBLING TREND ACROSS GENERATIONS

The NIH director also pointed to declining sperm counts as another area requiring further scientific investigation, suggesting that environmental exposures could be contributing to broader reproductive health concerns.

"But even more importantly, what are the factors, probably environmental factors, that have led to the decline in sperm counts, for instance? We need an answer to those questions," Bhattacharya said.

Bhattacharya said the NIH is investing in research to better understand the potential causes of those trends and determine how doctors should advise American men.

Christine said that testosterone is about more than muscle growth or physical appearance, arguing that hormone levels play an important role in men's overall health.

DEMS ROASTED FOR COMPARING HEGSETH'S TESTOSTERONE INITIATIVE TO 'GENDER-AFFIRMING CARE'

"Testosterone levels in men are absolutely related to their overall well-being, to their lifespan, to their health span, and to their wellness," Christine said.

He also noted that men with low testosterone tend to experience higher rates of anxiety and depression.

The administration is also developing separate hormonal health guidance for female service members, which the Defense Health Agency said would follow the September guidelines issued for male troops, with women's health specialists contributing to the recommendations, Christine said.

Christine said that the goal is ensuring that service members are equipped to perform their duties while addressing broader health challenges affecting American men.

"If we truly want our men who are in uniform to be at their best," Christine said, the focus must be on their ability to function and perform their jobs.

item.title: Pennsylvania law requires delivery robots to yield to pedestrians, yet protester still faced arrest
item.description: Carolyn Marvin, a 78-year-old retired professor, was arrested after blocking an Uber Eats delivery robot on a Philadelphia sidewalk for months.
item.content:encoded:
Most people see a food delivery robot rolling down the sidewalk and simply walk around it. But one Philadelphia woman decided she wasn't moving. She stood directly in front of an Uber Eats delivery robot, refusing to let it continue. Police eventually arrived, and the 78-year-old retired professor ended up in handcuffs.

Her protest has now sparked a much bigger conversation about robots taking over human jobs and how much space these machines should get on our sidewalks. And there's a surprising detail about Pennsylvania law that makes this whole situation even more interesting.

Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Join us Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com.

WORKERS ERUPT OVER DC PLAN TO BRING ROBOTAXIS TO CITY STREETS: ‘THIS IS BULLS---’

On Oct. 14, Carolyn Marvin, a retired University of Pennsylvania professor, was leaving a flu shot appointment in Center City Philadelphia when she spotted an Uber Eats delivery robot. Instead of stepping aside, she positioned herself in front of the machine near Reading Terminal Market on Filbert Street. Police reportedly responded after witnesses reported a disturbance. Officers said Marvin repeatedly refused instructions to move out of the robot's path. They eventually arrested her and issued her a disorderly conduct citation.

The encounter was captured on video and quickly attracted attention online. However, Marvin wasn't surprised by the attention. She had been deliberately blocking delivery robots for months, turning what might look like a strange sidewalk encounter into her own form of public protest.

In an interview with PhillyVoice, Marvin explained that she believes corporations are using autonomous machines to displace human delivery workers. She argued that her actions fall under her First Amendment right to protest. Marvin was taken to police headquarters and later released. She said she plans to fight the citation in court and continue blocking delivery robots when she has the opportunity. She also encouraged others who oppose the machines to join her protests.

Marvin's frustration goes beyond having robots share the sidewalk. She sees them as a direct threat to people who earn their living delivering food. Every order completed by a robot represents work that potentially could have gone to a human courier. That concern comes as more delivery companies experiment with automation to reduce operating costs.

Unlike a human courier, a robot doesn't collect tips or earn money for each delivery. Companies hope automation will eventually reduce operating costs, although the machines still require maintenance and monitoring.

However, whether Philadelphia's robot program has actually eliminated delivery jobs remains unclear. Uber has previously said its robots are intended to complement human delivery workers rather than replace them. Still, it's easy to understand why people who depend on delivery income might question how that arrangement will work as fleets expand.

Marvin also sees her protests as an opportunity to engage other pedestrians. She says people regularly stop to ask why she's blocking the machines. Those conversations are part of what motivates her to continue, even after her arrest.

You might assume that Marvin's arrest means delivery robots have the right of way on Philadelphia sidewalks. But Pennsylvania law offers a rather different answer.

The state's vehicle code classifies personal delivery devices as pedestrians and generally requires them to follow pedestrian traffic rules. However, the robots must yield the right-of-way or safely navigate around pedestrians and cyclists in pedestrian areas. That's an important detail. A delivery robot does not automatically have priority over someone walking down the sidewalk.

Of course, requiring robots to yield does not necessarily give people the legal right to deliberately obstruct deliveries. Police say Marvin refused repeated instructions to move after officers responded to a disturbance. Her disorderly conduct charge does not establish that robots have priority over pedestrians or settle whether her particular protest was legally protected.

Meanwhile, Pennsylvania law requires operators to notify municipalities at least 30 days before beginning delivery robot operations. Municipal officials can also prohibit the machines in areas where, after consulting the operator, they determine the robots would pose a hazard. That leaves an interesting question about how cities should handle future confrontations between pedestrians and commercial robots.

FOOD DELIVERY FAVORITE FORCED TO FORK OVER MILLIONS AFTER DOJ ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST AMERICAN WORKERS

Despite the controversy, companies continue investing in autonomous delivery because the technology offers some practical advantages. Uber Eats partnered with robotics company Avride to operate small, four-wheeled delivery machines that transport food over relatively short distances. The robots use cameras and sensors to navigate city streets. According to Avride, they travel at speeds of up to 5 mph and can carry up to 55 pounds of food or other goods.

The service launched in Philadelphia in March 2026. These robots can complete short deliveries without sending another car through traffic or requiring a courier to find parking. For customers, the convenience is obvious. Your food arrives inside a secure compartment that you unlock through the Uber Eats app. In Philadelphia, customers can reportedly opt out of robot delivery. However, availability and delivery options depend on the order and service area.

And the rollout is expanding. On Oct. 21, Avride announced an expansion of robot delivery in Philadelphia involving Wonder's Rittenhouse location and additional restaurants on the Grubhub platform. Robot delivery is now available from 25 Wonder restaurant concepts at the Rittenhouse location, with nine additional restaurants on Grubhub also participating. The company has not said whether the expansion will require more robots on Philadelphia sidewalks or whether its existing fleet will handle the additional orders.

Philadelphia's confrontation comes amid growing frustration with autonomous machines operating in public spaces. In September, we reported on a robot traffic jam in Chicago, where at least a dozen Coco delivery robots clustered along a sidewalk. The company blamed a deployment error and said it corrected the problem.

The incident raised concerns about pedestrian accessibility, particularly for people who use wheelchairs or mobility aids. A blocked sidewalk can create a serious obstacle for someone who cannot easily move into the street or squeeze past a machine.

Philadelphia has experienced its own robot mishaps. In April, a woman reported that an Uber Eats delivery robot bumped into her from behind near 15th and Locust streets. Li Gordon-Washington reportedly suffered a scratch and later struggled to determine which agency should handle her complaint. Avride acknowledged that its robot made minor contact with her while completing a turn.

These incidents help explain why some residents are losing patience. While the machines may be designed to navigate around people, they still have to handle unpredictable human behavior and crowded public spaces.

Delivery robots may soon become a familiar part of your neighborhood, especially if you live near busy restaurants or shopping districts. You could find yourself sharing sidewalk space with machines carrying someone else's dinner. That raises practical questions about safety and accessibility, along with concerns about jobs.

If you encounter a robot blocking a curb ramp or creating a hazard, keep your distance and report the problem to the operator or local authorities. In Pennsylvania, delivery robots must display operator identification and contact information. Documenting the location and the robot's identification number can help officials investigate a complaint.

There's also an opportunity for residents to get involved before delivery robot programs expand. Local governments can evaluate where these machines operate and whether particular routes create safety hazards. Paying attention to those decisions gives communities a chance to have a say in how their sidewalks are used.

For people whose livelihoods depend on deliveries, the questions run deeper. They deserve clear information about how companies plan to use automation and what that could mean for future work opportunities.

I've covered plenty of robots that can do impressive things, and I can appreciate the technology behind these delivery machines. But I never expected to see a 78-year-old retired professor arrested after refusing to let one deliver somebody's lunch. What really caught my attention was Pennsylvania's law requiring robots to yield to pedestrians. That makes the confrontation even more thought-provoking.

I understand why police would respond when a public dispute escalates, and I certainly wouldn't encourage anyone to interfere with a delivery. At the same time, I understand Marvin's frustration. We're watching companies introduce machines that can perform work people have traditionally been paid to do, and we still don't have clear answers about how many jobs could eventually disappear.

I think companies introducing this technology need to be much more transparent about its impact on workers. And when they want to operate on public sidewalks, residents deserve a genuine say in how that happens. I hope this incident encourages a serious conversation about those issues before another confrontation ends with someone in handcuffs.

If delivery robots make food delivery more convenient but eventually cost human workers their jobs, should cities still allow them to operate on public sidewalks? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

item.title: Yogurt shop murders fuel family questions about accomplice as rage lingers over wrongfully accused
item.description: Shawn Ayers, whose sister died in the 1991 Austin yogurt shop murders, co-founded the National Cold Case Center to help solve unsolved homicides.
item.content:encoded:
Nearly 34 years after his 13-year-old sister died during the 1991 Austin, Texas, yogurt shop massacre, Shawn Ayers and his wife, Angie, have launched a national cold case effort while still seeking answers about the attack and whether an accomplice is out there.

Angie, along with Shawn, whose sister Amy was among four girls killed in the attack, have joined former prosecutors Mindy Montford and Anne Marie Schubert to establish the National Cold Case Center.

The decades-long search for answers in Amy’s case inspired the couple to help establish the nonprofit, which helps to fund unsolved homicide investigations, train investigators and support victims’ families.

FORENSIC GENEALOGY UNMASKS COLD CASE SUSPECT AS STRANGLER, SEXUAL PREDATOR DECADES LATER: OFFICIALS

"Due to what we've gone through and seen, not only from our own experience, but from listening to other families struggle throughout this process," Angie told Fox News Digital. "Years ago, we had wanted to start a nonprofit."

Amy, Jennifer Harbison and Eliza Thomas, both 17, and Jennifer’s sister, Sarah Harbison, 15, died in the attack at the I Can’t Believe It’s Yogurt! shop on West Anderson Lane on Dec. 6, 1991.

On the night of the killings, Jennifer and Eliza were working the closing shift, while Sarah and Amy waited for them to finish so the four could head to a sleepover.

Shortly before midnight, authorities received a report of a fire at the shop. The blaze and water from the sprinklers altered the crime scene and diluted evidence, according to FBI files.

Inside, police discovered Sarah, Eliza and Jennifer stacked together in the shop’s storage room. They were stripped, gagged and bound with their own undergarments, and then shot in the back of the head with .22-caliber bullets.

Investigators found Amy in a separate area with a ligature around her neck and burns covering up to 30% of her body, according to court documents.

DNA FROM CHEWING GUM NAILS LONGTIME SEXUAL PREDATOR DECADES AFTER REIGN OF TERROR: REPORT

FBI records described two gunshot wounds: an initial .22-caliber shot that missed Amy’s brain and a second shot from a .380-caliber pistol through her cheek and jawline.

Investigators recovered a .380 cartridge casing in a floor drain. During the autopsy, officials recovered four .22-caliber bullets from the bodies.

The search for answers stretched across decades, combined with false confessions, arrests, convictions and appeals before DNA and ballistics evidence identified serial killer Robert Eugene Brashers in September 2025.

Brashers fatally shot himself during a January 1999 police standoff in Missouri, leaving the families no chance to confront him at a murder trial.

CALIFORNIA AUTHORITIES IDENTIFY FINAL UNKNOWN VICTIM OF ‘HAPPY FACE KILLER’ KEITH JESPERSON AFTER 34 YEARS

Authorities had previously connected him to other violent crimes, including killings in South Carolina and Missouri.

According to Austin police, Brashers used the same .380-caliber handgun in the yogurt shop murders to kill himself during the Missouri standoff.

For the Ayers family, identifying Brashers didn’t answer whether someone else participated in the yogurt shop killings. Angie questioned whether another perpetrator may have been involved, since two weapons were used during the attacks.

"I may be incorrect, but I don't think that I am," Angie told Fox News Digital. "There's never been an instance where he [Brashers] used both of those guns in his other cases."

DETECTIVES' TRUE CRIME PODCAST TAKES FRESH SHOT AT KILLER WHO VANISHED AFTER CAUGHT-ON-CAMERA MURDER

"There has been absolutely no definite answer on whether or not he was by himself, or had an accomplice.

"So, to us, we still don't have all the answers, and knowing that this case is still ongoing, I don't think anyone can say that they know exactly what happened because we can't ask."

Years before identifying Brashers, Austin investigators focused on four local teens: Robert Springsteen, Michael Scott, Maurice Pierce and Forrest Welborn.

Austin police arrested all four in 1999. Springsteen and Scott confessed during police questioning but recanted before trial, saying investigators pressured them into giving false statements.

Travis County juries convicted Springsteen of capital murder in 2001 and Scott in 2002. Springsteen received a death sentence, while Scott received life in prison.

The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals overturned Springsteen’s conviction in 2006 and Scott’s in 2007.

DNA testing failed to match any of the men to the crime scene. A judge released Springsteen and Scott in June 2009, and prosecutors moved to dismiss the charges that October.

Pierce proclaimed innocence but implicated Welborn. In 1991, he wore a police wire and tried to coax Welborn into confessing. An Austin police officer reported that Welborn denied any involvement. Welborn later passed a polygraph test.

Welborn never went to trial. When two grand juries failed to indict him, authorities dropped the case against him in 2000.

By then, he had spent months behind bars.

"I’m still really upset and mad at them. If they didn’t confess to something they didn’t do, we wouldn’t be here right now doing this today," Welborn told Texas Monthly.

Austin police officers arrested Pierce in 1999 on capital murder charges. Prosecutors dismissed Pierce’s charges in 2003, citing insufficient evidence, after he spent more than three years in jail.

In 2010, an Austin police officer fatally shot Pierce in 2010 following a traffic stop. Pierce fled the scene on foot and stabbed an officer in the neck with a knife, prompting authorities to open fire.

After investigators linked Brashers to the killings, Travis County Judge Dayna Blazey declared the four men innocent on Feb. 19, 2026. Months later, the Austin City Council approved a $35 million settlement covering the three surviving men and Pierce’s family.

Welborn initially rejected the city’s apology, saying that he lost an auto-repair business while incarcerated and endured years of public ostracism.

"Their apology is not accepted," he told Texas Monthly. "Their apology means nothing to me."

Welborn later said "it felt good" to have closure, although he wanted some of the detectives who worked the case "to go do some prison time."

None of the detectives have faced criminal charges in the case, Texas Monthly reported.

The Ayers couple said neither they nor the men or their relatives have contacted the other side.

"We haven't reached out and they have not reached out," Angie said.

Welborn could not immediately be reached for comment.

The Austin Police Department and Travis County District Attorney’s Office did not respond to requests for comment by publication.

Their experience seeking answers in Amy’s case, and hearing other families describe similar struggles, prompted Shawn and Angie to consider starting a nonprofit years ago.

"The frustrating part is being told no, but yet someone somewhere leaks the information and you're the last one to know when you should have been first and that is still happening today," Shawn told Fox News Digital, recalling his sister’s case.

Their partnership with Montford began in 2017, when they met with prosecutors about the yogurt shop killings. Montford, a Travis County assistant district attorney at the time, promised to stay with them.

"She made it a point to tell us that she was going to stick with us no matter what until the end," Angie said.

Montford then connected with Schubert, a former California prosecutor who helped bring the Golden State Killer to justice. The Ayers couple met Schubert at a 2023 cold case conference in Marble Falls, Texas, where the idea for the nonprofit took shape.

Now, they want to help other families find that kind of support.

SEND US A TIP

"It is up and running now... to provide funding and training for law enforcement, to have tools that they need to investigate cold cases, to be able to collect and report accurate data on unsolved cases, and connect law enforcement agencies around the world, and to have peer to peer family support and communication," Angie added.

GOT A TIP?

"Right now, funding is a, for us is a big thing, so we can get the first cases up and running."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Shawn said they have spread awareness by attending cold case conferences in several states, including California, Florida, Missouri, and North Carolina.
